title: Public vs Private vs Hybrid Cloud

content.title: Public vs Private vs Hybrid Cloud

blocks.content: The previous topic introduced three deployment models in a single overview table. Each deserves more than one row. This topic gives all three the direct, side by side, full depth comparison already promised.
1. Public vs Private vs Hybrid, Given Its Own Full Depth
blocks.text: 1. Public vs Private vs Hybrid, Given Its Own Full Depth

blocks.content: Public cloud, private cloud, and hybrid cloud each represent a genuinely distinct answer to where infrastructure lives and who shares access to it, and choosing correctly among them requires understanding each one's real, concrete tradeoffs in depth.

This topic examines each model individually before bringing them together in a single, practical decision framework, extending the brief overview table from the previous topic into genuine, actionable understanding.

Every example in this topic assumes the definitions already established in the previous topic: public cloud shares provider infrastructure, private cloud dedicates infrastructure to one organization, and hybrid cloud combines both.
By the end of this topic, choosing among the three for a genuinely new, unfamiliar workload should feel like a straightforward, structured evaluation rather than a vague, intuition driven guess.
https://algorithmxlr8-assets-images.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/devops-content-images/1784736033444-640541774.png
blocks.alt: Public vs private vs hybrid cloud given its own full depth

blocks.content: 2. Public Cloud in Full Depth

Public cloud, the model AWS itself directly provides and the primary focus of this entire course, offers the fullest realization of every benefit covered in the Why Cloud topic: maximum elasticity, minimal operational burden, and the broadest global reach.

The tradeoff is shared infrastructure: your workloads run on hardware also serving other customers, isolated through virtualization and AWS's own security controls, covered fully in the Shared Responsibility Model topic later in this module.

For the overwhelming majority of workloads, without a specific regulatory or data residency requirement demanding otherwise, this shared infrastructure model presents no genuine practical concern, and its benefits far outweigh any theoretical isolation tradeoff.

Public cloud is the correct default starting point for a new workload, and moving away from it should require a specific, identifiable reason, rather than public cloud needing to justify itself as the default choice.
3. Private Cloud in Full Depth

Private cloud dedicates infrastructure entirely to a single organization, either physically on premises in that organization's own facility or hosted exclusively by a third party but never shared with any other customer's workloads.

This dedicated arrangement provides the strongest possible control and isolation guarantees, valuable for organizations with strict regulatory requirements, extremely sensitive data, or existing, heavily invested on premises infrastructure not yet ready to migrate.

The tradeoff is significant: private cloud generally loses much of the elasticity, cost efficiency, and reduced operational burden covered in the Why Cloud topic, since the organization still bears responsibility for the underlying dedicated infrastructure.

Private cloud is the right choice specifically when a genuine, identifiable requirement, most commonly regulatory or compliance driven, makes the shared infrastructure model of public cloud genuinely unacceptable, not as a default, cautious starting position.
4. A Real Public vs Private vs Hybrid Example
blocks.text: 4. A Real Public vs Private vs Hybrid Example

blocks.content: Consider a healthcare technology company building both a patient facing appointment scheduling application and a system storing genuinely sensitive protected health information subject to strict regulatory requirements.

The appointment scheduling application, handling no sensitive health data directly, runs entirely on AWS public cloud, gaining full elasticity for handling unpredictable patient traffic and minimal operational burden for the engineering team.

The protected health information system runs on private cloud infrastructure, specifically to satisfy a genuine regulatory requirement around data residency and access control that the company's compliance team has identified as non negotiable.

The two systems connect through a hybrid architecture, with the public facing application securely calling the private system's API when it genuinely needs to access protected data, giving the company the best fit for each system's actual requirements.

blocks.content: 5. Recap: The Three Model Overview, Now Given Full Depth
blocks.text: 5. Recap: The Three Model Overview, Now Given Full Depth

blocks.content: The previous topic introduced all three models in a single overview table, comparing control, cost efficiency, and typical use in brief, summary form, intentionally deferring the full depth treatment to this topic.

This topic has now delivered that promised depth for public and private cloud individually, and this topic's real example demonstrates hybrid cloud in genuine, concrete practice, building directly on both the definitions and the bank example from the previous topic.

Seeing this healthcare example alongside the earlier bank example should reinforce a consistent pattern: hybrid cloud is rarely a single, monolithic choice, but rather a deliberate combination of public and private cloud, each applied to the specific workload it fits best.

This pattern, examined here across two different industries with two different specific regulatory drivers, is genuinely representative of how hybrid cloud is applied across real organizations throughout the industry.
https://algorithmxlr8-assets-images.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/devops-content-images/1784736038970-558165616.png
blocks.alt: Recap of the three model overview, already covered above

blocks.content: 6. A Practical Decision Framework

Start with public cloud as the default, and only consider private or hybrid cloud when a specific, identifiable requirement makes public cloud's shared infrastructure model genuinely unacceptable for a specific workload.

The most common genuine driver for private or hybrid cloud is regulatory or compliance requirement around data residency or access control, exactly as demonstrated in both this topic's healthcare example and the previous topic's bank example.

A second, less common genuine driver is significant existing investment in on premises infrastructure not yet ready for full migration, where hybrid cloud allows gradual, lower risk migration rather than a single, high risk cutover.

In the absence of either of these two genuine drivers, defaulting to public cloud and revisiting the decision only if a specific new requirement emerges is the correct, low risk, high benefit approach for the overwhelming majority of workloads.

7. A Common Mistake: Hybrid as the Always Safe Default
blocks.text: 7. A Common Mistake: Hybrid as the Always Safe Default

blocks.content: A common mistake is treating hybrid cloud as the safest, most cautious default choice, reasoning that combining both models must be lower risk than committing fully to either one, without a specific requirement actually driving that combination.

This reasoning is genuinely backwards. Hybrid cloud introduces real, additional complexity, connecting and securing two distinct environments together, that a purely public cloud architecture never has to address at all.

Choosing hybrid cloud without a specific, identifiable driver, exactly the two genuine drivers covered in the previous section's decision framework, adds this real complexity for no corresponding benefit, making it a strictly worse choice than public cloud alone.

The correct instinct is the opposite of cautious hybrid by default: start simple, with public cloud alone, and add private or hybrid complexity only when a specific, genuine requirement actually demands it.
https://algorithmxlr8-assets-images.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/devops-content-images/1784736042353-633165173.png
blocks.alt: The mistake of treating hybrid cloud as the always safe default choice

blocks.content: 8. Hybrid Cloud Connectivity in AWS

AWS provides specific services purpose built for hybrid cloud connectivity, most notably AWS Direct Connect, offering a dedicated, private network connection between an organization's own infrastructure and AWS, and AWS Site to Site VPN, offering an encrypted connection over the public internet.

Both services are covered in full depth in the Networking module later in this course, and their existence is precisely why hybrid architectures like this topic's healthcare example and the previous topic's bank example are genuinely practical to build and operate on AWS.

Recognizing that AWS explicitly supports and provides dedicated services for hybrid connectivity reinforces that hybrid cloud, when genuinely warranted, is a first class, well supported pattern, not an awkward workaround forced onto AWS's public cloud model.

This connectivity foundation is worth keeping in mind now, even though its full technical depth is deferred to the Networking module, since it explains concretely how the architectural pattern introduced in this topic is actually implemented in practice.
9. Comparing Private Cloud Options in Practice
blocks.text: 9. Comparing Private Cloud Options in Practice

blocks.content: Organizations choosing private cloud generally have two paths: building and operating truly on premises infrastructure themselves, or leasing dedicated, single tenant infrastructure hosted by a third party but never shared with any other customer.

The on premises path offers maximum control but requires the organization to handle every operational burden itself, physical security, hardware maintenance, and capacity planning, none of which the cloud computing benefits from the Why Cloud topic apply to.

The dedicated third party hosting path offers a middle ground, removing some physical operational burden while still providing the isolation guarantee that defines private cloud, though generally at a higher cost than shared public cloud infrastructure.

Understanding these two private cloud sub options is useful for correctly interpreting real world architecture discussions, where private cloud is sometimes used loosely to describe either path without distinguishing between them explicitly.
10. Compliance Frameworks That Commonly Drive This Decision
blocks.text: 10. Compliance Frameworks That Commonly Drive This Decision

blocks.content: Certain regulatory and compliance frameworks recur constantly as the genuine driver behind private or hybrid cloud decisions, including healthcare specific regulations protecting patient data, financial services regulations, and government specific security requirements.

AWS itself maintains compliance certifications against many of these frameworks for its public cloud infrastructure, meaning public cloud is often compliant by default for many requirements, narrowing the specific cases where private cloud is genuinely mandated rather than merely assumed necessary.

This is precisely why the decision framework covered earlier in this topic emphasizes identifying a specific, genuine requirement, since many organizations initially assume a compliance requirement mandates private cloud when AWS's own public cloud compliance certifications already satisfy it.

Verifying this directly against AWS's own published compliance documentation, rather than assuming private cloud is required based on a general impression of a regulatory framework, is a genuinely valuable, cost saving verification step.
11. A Third Real Example: Government and Public Sector
blocks.text: 11. A Third Real Example: Government and Public Sector

blocks.content: Government agencies and public sector organizations frequently have some of the strictest data residency and security requirements of any industry, making deployment model choice a particularly high stakes decision in this specific sector.

AWS operates specific, dedicated Regions built specifically to meet government sector compliance requirements, an example of how public cloud providers increasingly build purpose specific offerings to serve even the most stringent regulatory environments directly.

This pattern, a specialized version of public cloud built specifically for a compliance heavy sector, is worth knowing about as it demonstrates that the public versus private divide is not always a strict binary, but sometimes a spectrum of increasingly specialized public cloud offerings.

Recognizing this spectrum reinforces the practical decision framework covered earlier in this topic: the right answer often requires researching what specific, purpose built options a provider like AWS already offers before assuming private cloud is the only path to compliance.
12. Revisiting the Decision as an Organization Evolves
blocks.text: 12. Revisiting the Decision as an Organization Evolves

blocks.content: A deployment model decision made early in an organization's life is rarely permanent. A workload that started on private cloud due to a since resolved regulatory concern may later be a strong candidate for migration to public cloud once that concern no longer applies.

Conversely, a workload that started on public cloud may later develop a genuine new regulatory requirement, prompting a deliberate move to private or hybrid cloud, exactly the kind of specific, identifiable driver the decision framework in this topic calls for.

Treating this as a decision worth periodically revisiting, rather than a permanent, one time choice made at a workload's initial creation, keeps an organization's overall deployment model architecture aligned with its actual, current requirements.

This periodic revisiting mirrors similar advice already given for the broader Ingress versus LoadBalancer decision in an entirely different context, underscoring that architectural decisions throughout this kind of infrastructure work are rarely permanent and are worth reconsidering as circumstances change.
13. Best Practices for Choosing Among the Three Models
blocks.text: 13. Best Practices for Choosing Among the Three Models

blocks.content: Default new workloads to public cloud, treating it as the standard, expected starting point rather than something that needs to be specifically justified against private or hybrid alternatives.

Identify and document the specific, genuine driver, regulatory, compliance, or existing infrastructure investment, before choosing private or hybrid cloud for any given workload, avoiding the always safe default mistake covered earlier in this topic.

Use AWS's purpose built hybrid connectivity services, Direct Connect and Site to Site VPN, rather than improvising a custom, less secure connection between environments when a genuine hybrid architecture is warranted.

Revisit deployment model decisions periodically as regulatory requirements, business needs, and existing infrastructure investments evolve, rather than treating an early decision as permanently fixed.

blocks.content: 14. The Single Most Valuable Takeaway

Public cloud is the correct default, offering the fullest realization of cloud computing's benefits, and private or hybrid cloud should be chosen only when a specific, genuine requirement, most commonly regulatory or compliance driven, actually demands it.

Hybrid cloud is not an inherently safer, more cautious default. It introduces real additional complexity that is only worth accepting when a specific driver genuinely justifies it, exactly as covered in this topic's common mistake section.

The next topic, IaaS, PaaS, SaaS, introduces a genuinely distinct question from everything covered in this module so far: not where infrastructure lives, but how much of the technology stack you manage yourself versus your provider manages for you.

Keep both this topic's healthcare example and the previous topic's bank example in mind. Together they demonstrate the same underlying pattern across two different industries: deliberate, workload specific placement, not a single blanket choice.
This topic is now fully covered; IaaS, PaaS, SaaS, introducing a genuinely different question about how much of the stack you manage yourself, follows immediately next.
The where question, covered across the last three topics of this module, is now complete.
Every real world deployment model decision covered in this topic assumed a specific, genuine driver, never habit alone.
Carry that same deliberate reasoning forward into the how question this next topic opens.
This same evaluation discipline will recur throughout every architectural choice covered in the rest of this course.
IaaS, PaaS, SaaS: a spectrum, not three isolated boxes.
Default to the layer that matches genuine need, never the layer that is merely familiar.

blocks.title: Public vs Private vs Hybrid Cloud In Full
points: Public cloud offers the fullest realization of cloud computing's benefits and should be the default starting point for new workloads.
Private cloud offers the strongest control and isolation, appropriate specifically when a genuine regulatory or compliance requirement demands it.
Hybrid cloud deliberately combines both, applied per workload based on that workload's specific requirements, not chosen reflexively as a safer default.
The practical decision framework is simple: default to public cloud, and move to private or hybrid only with a specific, identifiable driver.
IaaS, PaaS, SaaS, covered next, introduces a distinct question: not where infrastructure lives, but how much of the stack you manage yourself.
